pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Why must the data be sorted before binary search, and where exactly in the algorithm does it rely on that?
expected_points: the discard step is a proof: everything left of a smaller element is also smaller only when data is sorted
on unsorted data the discarded half may contain the target, so a wrong answer is returned confidently
one comparison against the middle eliminates half the candidates only because order is guaranteed

questions.prompt: A sorted slice holds a million elements. Roughly how many probes does binary search need and why? What happens to that count when the slice doubles?
expected_points: about 20, because each comparison halves the candidates: n, n/2, n/4, ... 1
the number of halvings to reach one candidate is log2(n)
doubling the data adds just one more probe

questions.prompt: Name the two classic binary-search implementation bugs and how you defend against each.
expected_points: off-by-one / non-shrinking interval: lo = mid instead of mid+1 loops forever, hi = mid-1 under a half-open convention skips an unexamined index
defense: pick one interval convention, state the invariant, argue every update strictly shrinks the interval
midpoint overflow: (lo+hi)/2 can overflow fixed-size integers even when the result fits (the nine-year JDK bug)
defense: lo + (hi-lo)/2 computes the same midpoint without the overflowing sum

questions.prompt: Binary search is O(log n), yet sometimes plain linear search is the right choice. When, and why?
expected_points: unsorted data with one lookup: sorting first costs O(n log n), more than one O(n) scan
tiny n: constants and simplicity dominate; Big-O describes growth, not small-input speed
linked structures: no O(1) random access, so jumping to the middle costs O(n) anyway
many lookups flip the answer: sort once and every search becomes O(log n)

questions.prompt: Your sorted slice has a long run of duplicates of the target. Why doesn't the plain loop's return-on-equality give you the first occurrence, and what does the variant change?
expected_points: mid can land anywhere inside the run, so which occurrence you get is accidental
walking left from a match is O(n) worst case (imagine the whole slice equal to the target)
instead search for the boundary: the first index with xs[i] >= target, halving until the interval is empty
then verify the landing index is in range and actually holds the target

questions.prompt: You already keep the data in a hash table with O(1) lookup. What kinds of queries still need sorted data and binary search?
expected_points: order questions: first element >= x, everything between a and b, nearest value, predecessor/successor
hashing scatters keys and destroys order, so it only answers exact-match questions

questions.prompt: Binary search with no target value at all: what does searching over a yes/no condition look like, and what must be true of the condition?
expected_points: the answers over the range must be monotone: false...false true...true, never flipping back
you binary-search for the flip boundary, e.g. first commit where the build breaks
Go's sort.Search is exactly this shape: first index where a predicate is true
